paper_title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Gaussian avatars reconstruct persons geometry and appearance and animate the result using driving pose sequence (Qian et al., 2024; Kocabas et al., 2024). In applications such as AR/VR and sports (Hu et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025), users may need to edit an avatars appearance or inspect its motion. Clothing transfer and appearance editing (Lin et al., 2024; Ho et al., 2023), for example, require selecting the body part or garment to modify (Where). Inspecting that region during particular pose or motion also requires finding the intervals in which that pose or motion occurs (When). language query can describe both, but the avatar has no part or garment labels on its Gaussians and no motion labels on its frames. We therefore introduce avatar referring segmentation: 3D query selects the described region (Fig. 1(a)), while 4D query also selects the intervals that match the specified pose or motion (Fig. 1(b)). In reconstructed scenes, language Gaussian splatting already selects regions and relevant time intervals. In 3D, these methods attach image-language features to Gaussians and select regions whose features match query (Qiu et al., 2024). These features are learned per scene as language field in LangSplat (Qin et al., 2024) or registered directly in Dr. Splat (Kim et al., 2025), whereas ReferSplat (He et al., 2025) learns per-scene referring features from annotated expressions. To also determine when query is relevant, 4-LEGS (Fiebelman et al., 2025) grounds video-text features in dynamic Gaussians, while 4D LangSplat (Li et al., 2025) learns temporal language field from captions generated by multimodal large language model (MLLM). For humans, OpenHuman3D (Suzuki et al., 2025a) segments body parts and garments with CLIP image encoder fine-tuned on human parsing data, and OpenHuman4D (Suzuki et al., 2025b) tracks part masks over time. Despite these advances, enabling language querying on Gaussian avatars presents two challenges. The first is region ambiguity. Human parts and garments lie close together and often overlap. As the pose or viewpoint changes, different boundaries become visible. Feature-matching methods (Qin et al., 2024) rely on class-agnostic SAM masks (Kirillov et al., 2023), which do not necessarily follow these boundaries, and on generic CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) features, which poorly distinguish body parts and garments (Suzuki et al., 2025a). Replacing the SAM masks with human-parser masks improves the overall accuracy of LangSplat and Dr. Splat, but leaves their CLIP-based matching unchanged. Queries may also refer to part or garment indirectly, through its relation to another region or its function, and CLIP-based matching remains unreliable for such references in our evaluation (Tab. 2). The second is motion ambiguity. Even after the target region is identified, locating the intervals of fine-grained pose or motion remains difficult (e.g., Select the upper clothing while both upper arms lift outward until they are parallel to the ground in Fig. 1(b)). Mask tracking (Suzuki et al., 2025b) keeps the clothing selected over time but does not determine when the arms meet this condition. RGB-based methods can localize intervals (Fiebelman et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), but different motions can look alike in RGB frames while differing in their dynamics (Yang et al., 2026), and even video MLLMs struggle with fine-grained motion understanding (Hong et al., 2025). Gaussian avatars, however, already provide structure suited to both challenges. Each Gaussian is defined in canonical space and deformed to every pose (Qian et al., 2024), so it keeps its identity as the avatar moves. The driving pose sequence also provides joint trajectories. Building on this structure, we introduce HumanSkill-4D, which organizes avatar-specific knowledge and shared procedures into an agent skill (Tang et al., 2026) for frozen MLLM. The skills knowledge lies in per-avatar memories of the Gaussians in each part or garment and of joint trajectories. Its procedures are geometric operators that check pose and motion conditions and are shared across avatars. Specifically, to address region ambiguity, we accumulate labels from 2D human parser (Khirodkar et al., 2026) across views and poses into category scores that link body parts and garments to the avatars Gaussians. semantic memory combines these scores with category names and MLLMgenerated appearance descriptions. Given query, the MLLM uses the names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function, rather than matching the query to CLIP features, and the Gaussians linked to these categories form the selected region. For motion ambiguity, we store the driving joint trajectories in motion memory and check query conditions on them rather than on RGB frames. The checks use geometric operators adapted from PoseScript (Delmas et al., 2022), which describes poses by relations between joints, and MotionScript (Yazdian et al., 2025), which extends these relations to motion. Given 4D query, the MLLM composes these operators into program by linking them with temporal relations, and running it on the trajectories gives the matching intervals. In Fig. 1(b), for example, the program keeps the outward movements of both upPreprint per arms that end parallel to the ground. Because the MLLM chooses categories and operators rather than regions or intervals, each selection can be traced to these choices, and new motion conditions only require composing existing operators and relations or adding new ones. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks for selecting regions and pose or motion intervals. HumanSkill-4D performs best in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation. We make four contributions: (1) we introduce avatar referring segmentation and HumanSkill-4D, training-free framework that gives the structure of Gaussian avatars to frozen MLLM as skill, making its decisions traceable; (2) to address region ambiguity, we build semantic memory that also supports part segmentation; (3) to address motion ambiguity, we localize motions on joint trajectories with MLLM-composed programs, extensible by composing or adding operators and relations; and (4) to evaluate this task, we introduce three benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D is the most accurate on all three, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 3D language Gaussian splatting. Most language Gaussian methods select regions by matching query to CLIP features that are learned per scene (Qin et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024) or registered without per-scene optimization (Kim et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2026). Beyond object names, ReferSplat (He et al., 2025) learns per-scene referring features from annotated expressions, and ReLaGS (Xie et al., 2026) adds relation-guided retrieval. Open-vocabulary part segmentation likewise matches text to language-aligned features of 3D shapes (Ma et al., 2025) and humans (Suzuki et al., 2025a). Whereas these methods match queries to language features, HumanSkill-4D uses an MLLM to interpret region queries through semantic memory of avatar parts and garments, supporting both referring and part segmentation. 4D language Gaussian splatting. Recent work extends language Gaussian splatting to dynamic scenes, where query specifies region and when it is relevant. 4D LangSplat (Li et al., 2025) and 4-LEGS (Fiebelman et al., 2025) learn temporal language features from MLLM-generated captions and video-text features, respectively, and ST4R-Splat (Meng et al., 2026) extends referring segmentation to 4D Gaussians. For humans, OpenHuman4D (Suzuki et al., 2025b) and 4D-DRESS (Wang et al., 2024d) parse human parts over time. However, these methods mainly rely on RGB evidence, in which different motions can look alike (Yang et al., 2026) and fine-grained motion remains hard to capture (Hong et al., 2025). HumanSkill-4D instead measures pose and motion conditions on the driving joint trajectories, so it can distinguish subtle differences, such as the direction and extent of movement, and return the queried region with its matching intervals using compact memory. Agent skills and executable procedures. Large language models increasingly solve complex or fine-grained tasks through supplied procedures rather than task-specific training. Some compose predefined actions or handlers (Khot et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2025), whereas others generate code over visual tools (Gupta & Kembhavi, 2023; Surıs et al., 2023). More recently, agent skills compile experience into reusable knowledge and procedures that accompany the query (Wang et al., 2024a; Tang et al., 2026), and this paradigm now extends to 3D spatial and 4D spatiotemporal reasoning (Li et al., 2026a; Sohn et al., 2026). Building on this paradigm, HumanSkill-4D gives an MLLM peravatar memories as knowledge and shared geometric operators and temporal relations as procedures, so new avatar needs only its memories, and new motion condition requires only composing existing procedures or adding new ones.

sections.content: 4.1 OVERVIEW Given language query, HumanSkill-4D selects the described region of an avatar and, for 4D query, every matching interval in its driving pose sequence. As shown in Fig. 2, the framework prepares reusable memories offline, then uses frozen MLLM ΦMLLM to interpret queries online. In the offline phase, we build semantic memory Msemantic that links body-part and garment categories to the avatars Gaussians through category scores pic registered from frozen 2D human parser Φparse. The memory also stores category-level appearance descriptions generated by ΦMLLM from multi-view images (Sec. 4.2). motion memory Mmotion stores joint and root trajectories for each driving pose sequence. registry shared across avatars provides reusable templates for checking pose and motion conditions, along with temporal relations that specify how these conditions overlap or follow one another in time (Sec. 4.3). sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 EVALUATION PROTOCOL Benchmarks. To evaluate avatar referring segmentation, we introduce three benchmarks by augmenting existing human datasets with referring queries and human-annotated targets, following prior evaluations (He et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). ZJU-Refer-3D extends ZJU-MoCap (Peng et al., 2021) with dense part annotations and 20 referring queries covering part names, appearance, wearing relations, and functions. HuMMan-Refer-4D extends HuMMan (Cai et al., 2022) by converting its fine-grained body-part motion descriptions (Zhang et al., 2023) into 20 referring queries, while ZJU-Refer-4D extends ZJU-MoCap with 20 queries in the same format. Construction and annotation details appear in Supp. Secs. B.1B.2. Metrics. For part segmentation, we report mean per-category IoU (mIoU), overall pixel accuracy (OA), and mean per-category recall (mAcc) (Suzuki et al., 2025a). For 3D referring segmentation, we report mIoU over queries (He et al., 2025). For 4D referring segmentation, vIoU evaluates region accuracy and timing jointly, penalizing both incorrect masks and extra or missed active frames (Li et al., 2025). We additionally report tIoU, precision, and recall to assess temporal selection septIoU measures overlap between predicted and annotated active arately (Fiebelman et al., 2025). frames. Precision is the fraction of selected frames annotated as active, and recall the fraction of annotated active frames selected (Supp. Sec. C.1). Implementation details. Comparisons share avatar reconstructions. We use frozen Sapiens21B (Khirodkar et al., 2026) as Φparse and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b) as ΦMLLM. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced avatar referring segmentation, which selects avatar regions and the intervals satisfying queried pose or motion conditions, and presented HumanSkill-4D, training-free framework that gives the structure of Gaussian avatars to frozen MLLM as skill. To address region ambiguity, its semantic memory links body-part and garment categories and appearance descriptions to persistent Gaussian regions, enabling direct and indirect region references. To address motion ambiguity, the MLLM composes geometric operators adapted from PoseScript and MotionScript into programs executed on the driving joint trajectories. Because the MLLM chooses categories and operators rather than regions or intervals, its selections are traceable, and new motion conditions only require composing existing operators and relations or adding new ones. Experiments on our three human-annotated benchmarks show that HumanSkill-4D selects regions and intervals most accurately, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar. Limitations and future directions are discussed in Supp. Sec. E. 9 Preprint

sections.title: B BENCHMARKS
sections.content: B.1 ZJU-REFER-3D ZJU-Refer-3D extends ZJU-MoCap (Peng et al., 2021) with two forms of human annotation. For part segmentation, nine subjects are annotated at eight frames in four held-out cameras, yielding 288 ground-truth (GT) masks over the 16 categories of Sec. A.1. For 3D referring segmentation, each query is evaluated on the 32 held-out images of its subject (Sec. F). B.2 4D REFERRING EVALUATION HuMMan-Refer-4D and ZJU-Refer-4D each contain 20 queries (Sec. F). In both benchmarks, each query has target mask in two held-out cameras for every active frame. For HuMMan, we select sequences showing movements of specific body parts with clearly identifiable starts and ends, and annotators convert the provided fine-grained motion descriptions (Zhang et al., 2023) into referring queries. Annotators then review each clip and manually determine the intervals satisfying the specified pose or motion conditions. ZJU-MoCap queries use the same format, and annotators determine their intervals in the same way.

sections.title: E LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
sections.content: Because HumanSkill-4D reuses frozen parser and shared registry, it needs no per-avatar training, but it selects regions only among the categories of Φparse and checks motion only with the templates in R. Details outside these categories, such as logo or watch, may therefore not be selectable, and motions outside these templates, such as dancing or carrying an object, may not be checked. Future work can extend both components within the same framework. For regions, finer segmenter such as SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2026), which segments objects named by short noun phrases, could be used alongside Φparse to register such details as categories. For motion, actions could be decomposed into part-level conditions, as in prior work on fine-grained human motion (Delmas et al., 2022; Yazdian et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025), or object-relative templates could be added given object trajectories. 23 Preprint Figure S5: Qualitative 3D referring segmentation on ZJU-Refer-3D. uses Sapiens2 masks.
